archetype.name: Playoff Team (possession-first)
archetype.definition: Utah drives play like one of the league's three best teams at 5-on-5 and rides a lethal power play, but bottom-tier goaltending and penalty killing keep its goal margin well short of what its territorial edge should produce.

report.headline: Elite shot share, bottom-two goaltending: Utah's ceiling sits in the crease
report.take:
Strip away the scoreboard and Utah looks like a heavyweight. It owns 58.4% of the 5-on-5 expected goals and 57% of the shot attempts, both third in the league. It puts 30.4 shots a game on net (4th) and allows 23.3 (5th). That is a team spending most of its nights in the other end, and it is a clear step up from last season's 52.4% expected-goals share. The blueline grades A+, anchored by Mikhail Sergachev (5th of 250 on the defense tab, 14 points in 23-plus minutes a night). The forward group grades A, with real depth: Barrett Hayton's line is winning 71% of the expected goals and Anders Lee's 66.4%.

The problem is what happens when the puck does get through. Utah's goalies have saved 8 goals fewer than expected, 31st in the league. The combined save percentage is .868 against a league average of .892. Karel Vejmelka sits at .878 and Sebastian Cossa at .820 in limited work. That is why a team allowing the fifth-fewest shots ranks only 23rd in goals against. Last season the same organization got +14.1 GSAx from its crease, so this is not who these goalies have to be, but it is who they have been for 12 games. A 66.7% penalty kill (29th) compounds it.

The record of 8-4-0 and a 109-point pace hide a softer recent picture. The goal differential sits at +6 for the season, but it is -3 over the last ten games. Over the last five, Utah has allowed 4.2 goals a game. Three of the last four wins finished 5-4, one of them in overtime, so the margins have been thin. Pts vs Goal Diff is only +1, though, so this is not a lucky team. It is a dominant-possession team bleeding goals at the back end. The offense is also leaning hard on a 38.1% power play, the league's best by a distance: 36 of the listed forwards' 79 points have come with the man advantage.

Where it heads depends on which extreme moves first. The power play will cool from 38%, and that will cost goals. The save percentage and the penalty kill are just as likely to climb toward normal, and the 5-on-5 control looks structural rather than fluky. If Vejmelka finds even league-average form, this is a top-five team on merit. If he doesn't, Utah is a strong possession club fighting through a lot of 5-4 nights.

strengths.title: Owns the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Utah ranks third in both expected-goals share and shot-attempt share, and it is top five in both shots for and shots against a game. This is the most durable kind of strength because it comes from play-driving, not percentages. It also extends through the lineup, with depth forwards like Hayton and Lee posting the best on-ice shares on the team.

strengths.title: A blueline that drives everything
strengths.body: The defense grades A+. Sergachev logs over 23 minutes a night with 14 points and ranks 5th at his position. MacKenzie Weegar and Nate Schmidt both sit above 62% in expected-goals share. A group this deep should keep suppressing chances even as the season wears on.

strengths.title: League-best power play
strengths.body: At 38.1%, Utah's power play leads the league by a wide margin over a 21.2% league average. Keller, Cooley and Guenther are driving it. That rate will not hold, but a unit generating this many shots should stay well above average even as it cools.

concerns.title: Goaltending is giving it back
concerns.body: A -8 team GSAx (31st) and a .868 save percentage (30th) explain why the fifth-fewest shots against turns into the 20th-most goals allowed a game. Last season's +14.1 GSAx suggests better is possible, but nothing in the sheet guarantees it. Until it turns, every lead is fragile.

concerns.title: Penalty kill near the bottom
concerns.body: The penalty kill is killing 66.7% of penalties, 29th and far below the 78.3% league average. It sat at 78.1% last season. Some of this is the goaltending again, which means it should mend alongside it rather than independently.

concerns.title: Recent results outrunning the margin
concerns.body: Utah has gone 6-4-0 over its last ten games but been outscored over that stretch. It has allowed 4.2 a game over the last five, nearly a goal above its season rate. The wins have come in shootout-style games that a cooling power play may not keep winning.

trend.note: Utah has strictly alternated wins and losses or stacked short runs, never losing two straight but never winning more than three. The underlying play has stayed dominant while goals against have crept up lately.

weekAhead.headline: Two contenders bracket two soft spots, three of four on road
weekAhead.body:
The week opens and closes against top-six teams on the site. Minnesota comes to Utah with the league's third-best defense, a .918 save percentage and A-grade goaltending, exactly the kind of crease that can neutralize Utah's shot volume. The trip ends in Toronto, where the Leafs' 95.2% penalty kill is the best in the league and directly blunts Utah's biggest weapon.

In between sit two very gettable road games. Pittsburgh's defense ranks 26th in points allowed to forwards above expectation and 29th against wingers. Philadelphia ranks 31st in expected-goals share and dead last in scoring. The Flyers' goalies are 5th in GSAx, though, so Utah may have to beat a hot netminder with volume. A 2-2 week is the floor; 3-1 is realistic if the crease holds up.

keyMatchups.title: Utah power play vs Toronto kill
keyMatchups.body: The league's best power play meets the league's best penalty kill on November 3. If Toronto shuts down the man advantage, Utah needs its 5-on-5 edge to carry the night. That edge should be there, since the Leafs are only 25th in expected-goals share.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume vs Minnesota's crease
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota allows only 21.7 shots a game and its defense holds forwards well under their averages, third-best in the league. Utah's possession edge will be tested against a team that also controls play. A low-event game puts even more weight on Vejmelka.

keyMatchups.title: Keller and Guenther vs Pittsburgh wings
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 29th in points allowed to wingers relative to expectation. That sets up well for Keller (15 points) and Guenther (35 shots, the team high). It is the best scoring spot of the week.

weekAhead.watch: Vejmelka's save percentage against Minnesota and Toronto: if it climbs, Utah's record will start matching its play.

restOfSeason.body:
The 5-on-5 dominance is the part to believe in: it comes from shot generation and suppression across the lineup and an A+ blueline, not from bounces. The power play at 38% will regress noticeably, which takes some goals off the board. The goaltending and penalty kill sit so far below average that normal variance alone should give a lot of them back, and last season's positive GSAx says this crease is capable of it. Netting those out, Utah should settle as a top-eight team in goal differential rather than ninth on a run of 5-4 games.

The 109-point pace is too rich given how thin the margins have been and how much the power play has carried. Something in the range of 98 to 108 points is a fair expectation, comfortably a playoff team in the Central, with a higher ceiling if Vejmelka steadies.
swingFactors: How far the power play cools
Penalty kill recovering toward league average

confidence.note: 12 games is small, but possession and shot-share numbers stabilize faster than save percentage.
